what_it_does: As chips age or are manufactured with slight imperfections, individual transistors can start misbehaving and producing wrong arithmetic results — a problem called hardware faults. Chips that run large AI language models (LLMs — programs that read and generate text) face this risk, and the usual fix is to run the chip at a safely slow speed with extra electrical headroom (voltage margin), or to use a costly technique called algorithm-based fault tolerance (ABFT) that checksums every computation. ReaLM observes that large language models are surprisingly forgiving of small numerical errors — a flipped bit in one multiplication rarely changes the final answer much. It therefore designs a lighter-weight version of ABFT that collects statistics about errors actually occurring on the chip at runtime, and only triggers a correction when the error is large enough to matter, avoiding the full cost of traditional ABFT. This co-design of the error-detection circuit with the model's natural error tolerance reportedly lets the chip run faster and more efficiently without sacrificing reliable output, though exact figures are not available from the abstract alone.
